# Independent audit: fiberwise constant fractional cap covers



Source: `candidate 05b459fea3722ebb`.
Independent example verifier: `supporting computation verify_fractional_incidence_examples_minkowski.py`.


the finite occupied-parity Helly argument for nonclosed convex sets.
The independently written Fraction-only verifier passed **79 exact
checks** of both displayed interval examples. These computations
verify the examples; the general theorem is justified by the proof
checks below. The author also reran this verifier and clarified that
the last example has an incidental two-cap global subcover.

## 1. Intrinsic setting and local constant incidence

The maximum affine dimension of the finitely many integer fibers is
q. Exactly the q-dimensional fibers contribute to H_q when q>=1,
and their finite positive intrinsic volumes sum to M. There is no
assumption that their affine direction spaces all coincide.

On one intrinsic fiber plane, an ambient halfspace restricts to a
proper halfspace, the whole plane, or the empty set. If it captures
full measure, closedness and the density of the body's interior imply
that it contains the entire body. Otherwise positivity of the
constant weighted incidence and finiteness imply the existence of a
proper cap of positive volume.

Its cutting hyperplane intersects the relative interior. A point can
be chosen on that section away from every noncoincident restricted
hyperplane. In dimension one, noncoincident hyperplanes are simply
different points, so the same selection works. On a sufficiently
small interior ball, all noncoincident indicators are constant and
the coincident indicators have one of two orientations. The weighted
incidence is constant on each open half-ball and agrees almost
everywhere with the same prescribed value; hence the two orientation
weights balance. Positivity of each coefficient guarantees an
oppositely oriented cap. That pair covers the whole fiber plane.

Thus the local cover of size one or two consists of original ambient
caps, even when their ambient normals differ and only their restricted
boundaries agree. No common pair across fibers is assumed.

## 2. Finite parity Helly proof

For a finite inequality system missing nonempty finite P, the minimum
over P of the maximum original violation is positive. Choosing eta
smaller than it makes the strict relaxed system still miss P. The
upper thresholds T_i are strictly above every a_i.p and the initial
relaxed threshold.

The admissible threshold set is closed: for each p, exclusion means
that at least one inequality t_i<=a_i.p holds, a finite union of closed
conditions. Intersecting these conditions over finite P and the closed
threshold box gives a compact nonempty set. Therefore the sum of
thresholds attains a maximum; no variational existence is assumed.

At a nonsaturated coordinate i, there must be an exclusive contact
p_i with a_i.p_i=t_i and all other inequalities strict. Otherwise,
among the finitely many points satisfying the other inequalities
strictly, either there is no point or every remaining obstruction at
coordinate i has a positive gap. A sufficiently small increase of
t_i would preserve exclusion, contradicting maximality. The contact
points are distinct. If two have the same parity, their midpoint is
in P and satisfies every strict inequality: at each contact's own
index the other contact has a strict inequality, and at every other
index both do. This is impossible. There are at most k nonsaturated
coordinates.

Every saturated inequality is strictly satisfied by every point of
P, so it contributes nothing to exclusion. The nonsaturated strict
inequalities exclude P; replacing them with their original stronger
closed inequalities preserves exclusion. This proves the inequality
version with the stated exact occupied-parity number.

For a polytope family, finite inequality descriptions and grouping
the selected inequalities by their parent polytopes are valid also
for lower-dimensional polytopes. An empty member is immediately a
one-set certificate. For arbitrary convex E, the finite polytope
conv(E intersect P) is contained in E and has exactly the same trace
on P. Thus replacing each convex set by this polytope loses neither
the initial emptiness nor the selected subfamily conclusion on P.
The argument indeed handles open or otherwise nonclosed convex sets.

The actual positive-fiber base is midpoint-closed: an integer midpoint
fiber contains the Minkowski midpoint of two positive q-fibers, whose
dimension is at least q. Since q is maximal among integer fibers,
that fiber has dimension exactly q and belongs to P. The same finite
Minkowski inclusion proves lattice completeness in conv(P), although
only midpoint closure is needed. These statements also hold for
lower-rank base sets and n=0.

## 3. Projection local-to-global cover

For a nonempty selected index set J, the set

    E_J = projection(C intersect all H_i^c, i in J)

is convex. Complements of the closed caps are open halfspaces;
projection need not preserve closedness, but the preceding Helly
lemma explicitly avoids any closedness requirement. At every actual
base z, absence from E_J is exactly the assertion that J covers the
entire fiber K_z. This equivalence involves the actual fiber of C,
not its centroid, its projection alone, or a replacement union.

If every positive fiber has a local cover using at most t caps, then
the intersection of the finitely many E_J misses P. Select at most
k of these convex sets by parity Helly. At each base at least one
selected E_J is absent, so its associated cap list covers that whole
fiber. The union of these lists contains at most kt original caps.
Overlaps between lists only reduce the count. Applying this with
t=2 proves the stated global subcover theorem.

## 4. Budget consequence, boundary mass, and partition case

The selected subcover includes every point of every positive fiber,
not merely almost every point. Its masses therefore sum to at least
M. Since there are at most 2k selected original caps, at least one
original cap has actual mass at least M/(2k). No multiplication of
budgets by the given coefficients occurs in this step, and the
constants b_z may vary with the base.

Whole-fiber boundary mass is retained by the one-cap branch: if the
ambient normal vanishes on a fiber direction and that fiber lies on
the boundary, the entire closed fiber belongs to the cap. Genuine
intrinsic cutting hyperplanes have zero H_q measure. The proof never
replaces closed caps by open caps in a measured assertion. Open
complements are used only for the exact set-theoretic projection
equivalence. Lower-dimensional fibers are null in the current q>=1
measure; covering them is not required or claimed.

For an almost-everywhere disjoint partition, unit coefficients give
constant incidence one on every positive fiber. Omitting any original
positive-mass cap from a subcover would leave positive measure
uncovered, because that cap overlaps the finite selected union only
on a null set. Hence all positive original caps are indispensable
and r<=2k even with full-fiber ownership. The theorem does not extend
the earlier stronger component count to this setting.

Because q>=1 implies d>=1, Gamma_d<=1/2 and k<=2^n give the stated
comparison with Gamma_d M/2^n. No q=0 theorem is asserted here.

## 5. Examples and exact sharpness

The symmetric binary-product example has k singleton parity classes.
The affine isolation margin is at least one away from its own binary
vertex; the strict coefficient choice makes each cap empty at every
other integer fiber. Opposite central cuts in the own fiber have
mass V/2 and only null overlap. Thus all 2k positive caps are necessary,
M=kV, and every budget equals M/(2k), including n=0.

For the full-ownership interval example, the endpoint Minkowski
midpoint is [2,4], contained in the stated middle interval [-1,5].
The convex hull therefore realizes exactly the three displayed
integer fibers. The cap-length rows are respectively

    (1,1,0,0), (0,0,4,2), (0,0,2,0).

Every excluded cap has strictly negative margin on the whole relevant
fiber, and the two within-fiber overlaps are only cut endpoints.
Global masses are (1,1,6,2), with total ten. There are two parities
but one midpoint component. Hence this is an exact counterexample
to r<=2c(P) or r<=2(k-1) once full ownership is allowed. It does not
claim equal budgets or a no-heavy condition.

For the eight-cap fractional example, upper and lower threshold
multisets coincide exactly at all three integer bases. On every open
interval between consecutive thresholds, their unweighted incidence
is four and weighted incidence is one. Every boundary point is also
covered; the larger incidence on these finitely many points is null.
All individual cuts are proper. The printed masses
(12,15,9,12) and (12,9,15,12) are correct, and their quarter-weighted
sum is M=24. Different slope sets preclude any globally coincident
opposite ambient hyperplanes. There happens to be a global two-cap
subcover x>=2z-1 and x<=z+1; the source now explicitly states this
and does not claim that this example requires four caps.

## Scope

The theorem solves the positive fiberwise-constant fractional-incidence
subclass, and its proof supplies an exact original-cap subcover.
Ordinary overlapping covers, including three centroid vertex caps
of a triangle, can have variable incidence inside one fiber and fall
outside its hypotheses. The proof makes no assertion that critical
cap stress in a general OC counterexample supplies constant incidence.
No general OC conclusion is inferred. This scope and every stated
constant pass the audit.
